extracted.intended_audience: journalists, infographic designers, and content creators producing web or print infographics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and applying the visual elements (colour, typography, icons, images, layout) that make an infographic clear, accessible, and visually harmonious for web and print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic use of colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour is arguably the most powerful visual tool in an infographic; it sets the tone, groups related information, separates sections, highlights key data, and influences how the audience feels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose colours that align with the subject matter and the emotional response you want. Use colour to group related content, separate sections, and draw attention to critical data points so the viewer can scan and understand structure quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Different hues carry psychological associations that affect how people think, feel, and behave (e.g., red = urgency/energy/passion; blue = trust/calm; green = growth/health/environment; yellow = optimism/attention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a palette whose emotional associations match the topic (e.g., calm blues/greens for health-awareness; avoid aggressive reds for sensitive topics). Use colour meaning intentionally rather than as decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Palette size and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-designed infographic typically uses a limited palette of three to five colours, with one or two base colours and a contrasting highlight colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid too many colours (creates visual noise). Use colour-theory schemes (complementary, analogous, triadic) to build palettes that balance contrast and harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour for grouping and hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour serves a structural role: the same colour can link related pieces of content; different background colours can separate sections; a single bright contrasting colour can mark the most important element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent colour assignments to indicate relationships and importance so viewers instantly see which data belong together and where to focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour accessibility and contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all viewers perceive colour the same way (≈8% of men and 0.5% of women have colour vision deficiency); relying only on red/green differences can exclude audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify text-to-background contrast ratios with tools like WebAIM’s Contrast Checker and avoid conveying meaning only via colour; ensure palettes meet accessibility standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font selection for readability and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Typography delivers textual content (numbers, labels, headings, explanations) and communicates mood and personality; the font choice signals whether the piece is playful, serious, or corporate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick fonts that are legible at the intended viewing size and that match the infographic's tone before viewers read a word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serif vs. sans-serif choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Serif fonts feel traditional and authoritative; sans-serif fonts appear clean, modern, and remain legible at smaller sizes—making sans-serif generally preferred for infographics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sans-serif for most body text and small sizes; consider a serif for a title to add gravitas when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Create clear text hierarchy with distinct styles for main heading, section headings, and body text so viewers can quickly find the main message, sections, and details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the main heading largest and most prominent; section headings smaller but distinct; body text smallest and most readable. Avoid similarly sized text across the infographic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-/three-font rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit font choices to two or three families at most (e.g., a bold, distinctive heading font paired with a clean body font).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using five or six different fonts (common beginner mistake) because multiple fonts compete for attention and destroy cohesion. Maintain consistent font sizes suitable for medium (print: body ≥10pt; digital: body ≥14pt; posters: scale up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Font personality must match content
rubrics_metrics.description: Fonts carry personality (rounded = friendly; sharp geometric = precise; handwritten = informal) and should match the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose typefaces appropriate to the topic (avoid Comic Sans for financial regulations; avoid stiff corporate type for children's guides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of icons for space efficiency and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Icons are simplified symbolic graphics that represent ideas, objects, or actions and can replace text to reduce clutter and make meaning instantly clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use icons to condense labels or concepts (e.g., smartphone icon next to a figure), break up text, and add visual rhythm, especially where space is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Icon consistency of style
rubrics_metrics.description: All icons within an infographic should look like they belong to the same family and share the same visual treatment (line-art, filled/solid, or flat design).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mixing hand-drawn icons with sleek corporate icons. Also ensure consistent colour usage and uniform scaling unless deliberate emphasis is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Icon stories (composed icon narratives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine multiple icons into small visual scenes that illustrate a concept or process (e.g., person + arrow + building = commuting to work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use icon stories to depict simple narratives or processes without text or photos, keeping visual language consistent and clean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use photographs sparingly and purposefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs add real-world example, emotional weight, or context but are visually complex and can compete with data and design elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include photos only when they serve a specific purpose; use sparingly; if unsure why a photo is included, leave it out to avoid clutter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use illustrations for control and abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations can be designed to match the palette, style, and tone, and are useful for representing abstract concepts that don't photograph well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer illustrations when you need stylistic control or to represent abstract ideas without introducing photographic visual noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image integration best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Images should directly support content, harmonize with the colour palette, and be high-resolution and appropriately sized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid decorative images with no informational purpose. Use colour overlays/filters to align photos with the palette. Don’t use pixelated or oversized images that dominate layout or undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual harmony across elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour, typography, icons, and images must support one another to tell a unified story so the design feels cohesive rather than disjointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a unified style guide so elements match in tone, colour, and treatment; when design is cohesive the viewer absorbs information without being distracted by design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual hierarchy of importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange design elements in order of importance so the most critical data is most visually prominent (via size, boldness, colour, placement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hierarchy to guide the viewer’s eye from top-level takeaways to supporting details; ensure supporting data is present but less dominant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of white space (negative space)
rubrics_metrics.description: White space is the empty area around and between elements; it prevents the infographic from feeling cramped and gives the eye room to rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally leave space to separate sections and improve readability; avoid overcrowding, which reduces comprehension and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall consistency across all elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency ties everything together—matching icon styles to the colour palette, complementary font styles, and images that belong to the same design world as charts and icons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow a unified style guide; mismatched fonts, icon styles, or photos create a disjointed, amateurish feel regardless of data quality.
